<strong>Les jeunes diplômés de Montréal: Recent graduates in Montréal often run into many difficulties when looking for their first job. The accounts of several of them allowed us to explore these obstacles and the strategies they adopted to overcome them.
La quête d’un premier travail est un par: The search for a first job is a path full of obstacles for recent graduates in Montréal. Jessica, 24, who graduated in security and police studies, is no exception. She wears a broad, warm smile. Her long, curly black hair, pulled back in a ponytail, frames an expressive face. Her assured tone hints at a quiet confidence and a clear desire to make things change. Although she finished her studies with solid training, she faced a much harder ordeal than she had imagined. “You leave university with a lot of theory in your head, but no practice,” she explains.
Après des mois de recherches infructueus: After months of fruitless searching, it was with the help of a contact that she was able to land an internship at a government organization.
\"Ce qui va aussi faire en sorte que tu: “What will also make you stand out is your contacts who are ready to refer you, because paper résumés aren’t enough,” she says.
Malgré un marché du travail qui semble s: Despite a job market that seems to be holding steady, the unemployment rate in the Montréal census metropolitan area stood at 7.1% in April 2025, according to the Institut de la statistique du Québec. For people with a bachelor’s degree, it was 4.8% nationwide in 2024. These statistics might suggest that recent graduates have less trouble finding a job at the end of their studies. But that would be jumping to conclusions. Why, despite a university education, is the search for a first job in Montréal a true uphill battle? What causes these young people the most difficulty, between a lack of professional network or a lack of experience?

Jenny, montréalaise de 24 ans elle aussi: Jenny, also a 24-year-old Montréaler, went through a job search quite similar to Jessica’s. Her sociable nature is obvious right away, as is her remarkable ease at making connections with others. Her attentive gaze betrays a great ability to listen. A business administration graduate, she ultimately found her current position through an acquaintance. “It’s by reaching out to all kinds of people and talking about my studies with an acquaintance that I was able to find my current job,” she says. Her determination to succeed professionally comes through in every word.

L’expérience et le réseautage, voilà deu: Experience and networking are two essential elements, she believes. “You really have to do as many internships as you can and also go to conferences to meet lots of people who are in the job market,” she advises. These events make it possible to widen your network, an aspect she considers crucial.
LinkedIn a aussi été un outil indispensa: LinkedIn was also an indispensable tool in her job search. She recommends making use of all the platform’s features to connect with as many professionals as possible.
Pour Louise-Josée, 25 ans, détentrice d’: For Louise-Josée, 25, who holds a bachelor’s degree in political science, the story is different. This young woman with a frank smile brings a touch of humour to her stories, and her contagious laugh instantly breaks the ice. She spent more than a year looking for a first job. A trying period. “I knew it was a bit difficult to find work with the degree I had, but I didn’t think it would be this hard,” she confides.
\"J’étais sur LinkedIn <em>every day,</e: “I was on LinkedIn every day, I was scrolling on LinkedIn more than I was on my socials,” she says, laughing. Despite her perseverance, she found this period extremely discouraging. “I had done everything by the book, working and studying, but I couldn’t find anything,” she says, a hint of despair in her voice. “I had physical repercussions from the stress of trying to find this job,” she confides.
Dans son cas, le réseautage n’a pas été: In her case, networking was not an effective solution.
L’élément clé qui l’a finalement aidée à: The key element that finally helped her land her job was tailoring her résumé to each posting and applying non-stop. “My advice is to apply as much as possible everywhere. If you can, apply 100 times a day,” she says, chuckling.

Laura Balan, coach de carrières, et Mehd: Laura Balan, a career coach, and Mehdi Bagma, president of the recruitment firm Kadmaco, come to the same conclusion. Many recent graduates don’t always adopt the best strategies in their search for a first job, they note. The problem often lies in their approach.
Le réseautage est une des clés de la réu: Networking is one of the keys to success, says Mehdi. “Your network is your net worth,” he says with conviction. “That doesn’t mean there are no job openings just because you don’t see any available; companies don’t always have the funds to post a position. That’s why you have to move forward. Nothing ventured, nothing gained,” he says. He therefore advises not waiting and always reaching out to recruiters. When it comes to networking, Laura stresses the importance of LinkedIn, but it isn’t the only way to build a network. For young people with no network, you have to take initiative, she advises. “They should be curious about the networking events organized by their university, look for these events on social media and use their school to access events that match what they’re looking for,” she says, optimistic.
Concernant les jeunes qui n’ont pas fait: As for young people who haven’t done an internship or who have no experience, “it’s not a problem,” she says confidently. “They just need to emphasize on their résumé the projects they worked on while they were still studying.” Even without experience, “soft skills”—interpersonal and behavioural skills—can make all the difference to an employer, she says, advice that proves valuable for those who doubt their abilities.
Selon Mehdi, on en revient à la question: According to Mehdi, it comes back to the chicken-and-egg question: “To work, you need experience, but to get experience, you need to work.” For him, it’s possible to make up for this lack of experience by highlighting transferable skills on your résumé. “You have to link some of the experiences you’ve had to the ones you’re trying to get; making connections between skills can make the difference,” he points out.

Candice Fuego, assistante, recruteuse et: Candice Fuego, an assistant, recruiter and human resources management specialist, also sheds light on the difficulties racialized recent graduates face in their job search.
« On connaît très bien l’enjeu du racism: “We know the issue of systemic racism and sexism very well,” she says. An issue brought to light in 2018 by Jean-Philippe Beauregard, then a sociology doctoral student. <l1>The research, conducted in Quebec</l1>, shows that a fictitious candidate named Marc-André has a 36% chance of being contacted for a job, compared with 12% for a fictitious candidate named Mamadou, with equal skills and degrees.
Pour Candice, il est donc crucial de res: For Candice, it is therefore crucial to stay focused on your professional skills in an interview and to avoid revealing too much about your personal life. However, even if you do everything you can to avoid experiencing these injustices by staying discreet, the final decision always rests with the manager, she points out. A hard but realistic observation, since even for an excellent candidate, some decisions can be influenced by unconscious bias.
Elle souligne également la pression cons: She also highlights the constant pressure to stand out: “I always think with the reality of systemic racism that’s there, and the fact that you have to stand out all the time.” In some companies, racialized people have to make more effort to get the same recognition as others, she adds. Once again, it all depends on the employer and its organizational culture.
Pour les jeunes diplômés racisés qui ne: For racialized recent graduates who don’t know where to start building their network, Candice advises activating their closest contacts: “It’s important to talk with your community, to find people who are already in the field that interests you, or even in other fields.” This makes it possible to build a network in a setting where you feel comfortable. She also recommends starting your professional experience within that same community, if possible, relying on social media, community pages, or platforms like Eventbrite to find relevant and interesting events. “You have to connect with people who are ready to help you or train you.”
Si le réseautage, la mise en avant des c: While networking, highlighting transferable skills and having a presence on LinkedIn are common tools, Candice points out that systemic racism demands extra effort from racialized recent graduates.
Louise-Josée, elle, est consciente de ce: Louise-Josée, for her part, is aware of this difficulty. “Systemic racism and employer bias can come into play, but when you’re further along in the hiring process, because without experience you just don’t get past the first step of being noticed by the employer,” she says. Today, with the experience she has accumulated, she continues her job search. “With my current job I’ve gained a bit of experience, but it’s not enough when I look at the job descriptions, I don’t know what the future holds for me so I’m still looking.”
